domains.title: Samshin, the Three Spirits
domains.subtitle: triple goddesses of childbirth and the destiny of children
domains.lead: Samshin is the triple spirits, often imagined as three grandmother goddesses, who govern childbirth and the fate of newborn children in Korean tradition. The name means "Three spirits" and belongs to the domain "Birth, Triple Spirits." Samshin means "three spirits" or "three gods" and refers to the deities who preside over conception, pregnancy, safe delivery, and the destiny of the child. In shamanic belief the three spirits may be distinguished as one who grants pregnancy, one who gives bones, and one who gives the soul; yet they are also worshipped as a single goddess, Samshin Halmoni.

cards.name: Three Goddesses

cards.name: Pregnancy and Birth

cards.name: Child's Destiny
cards.desc: Samshin is believed to weave or decree the life span, fortune, and character of the newborn.

cards.name: Household Shrine
cards.desc: A small domestic altar keeps the birth spirits present and honoured in family life.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Samshin is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Origin of Samshin
myths.text: A common shamanic narrative tells of a girl or a nun who encounters a Buddhist monk or the Buddha himself. Through a series of trials she becomes the mother of the three spirits, each of whom receives dominion over a different aspect of birth and fate.

myths.title: The Birthing Room Shrine
myths.text: Families placed a small shrine to Samshin Halmoni in the birthing room or near the mother's quarters. Offerings of rice, soup, and clean cloth were made to thank the spirits for a safe delivery and to ask for the child's long life.

myths.title: The Gut for a Child
myths.text: When a child fell ill or a woman had difficulty conceiving, a mudang (shaman) would perform a gut invoking Samshin. The ritual identified spiritual obstacles, offered petitions for health, and reconfirmed the bond between the family and the birth spirits.

etymology.derivation: The name is composed of 三 (sam, "three") and 神 (sin, "spirit, deity"). Read 삼신 in Korean, it denotes the triad of birth spirits. The honorific Halmoni (할머니, "grandmother") is often added as a term of affection and respect.

nameVariations.note: The figure addressed as Grandmother Samshin.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Samshin, the Hangul form is 삼신 and the Hanja form is 三神. Hangul ‘삼신’ and Hanja ‘三神’; the figure is also called Samshin Halmoni (삼신할머니). The ASCII form samshin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Samshin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Samshin illustrates the deep interpenetration of shamanic and Buddhist idioms in Korean religion. The origin myth often involves a Buddhist monk, while the rituals are performed by mudang. Confucian patriarchal culture domesticated the cult by placing it under the authority of the household, yet the figure of the powerful grandmother spirit preserves an older, female-centred theology. In modern Korea, Samshin Halmoni is remembered in childbirth customs, fertility prayers, and folk art, sometimes detached from explicit shamanic practice.
lore.culturalLegacy: Samshin remains one of the most emotionally resonant figures in Korean folk religion. New parents still encounter rituals and taboos associated with the birth spirits, and the image of Samshin Halmoni appears in folk paintings, shamanic altars, and contemporary media about Korean shamanism. The figure also informs feminist readings of Korean religion, which highlight the persistence of female divine power within a patriarchal society. Medical and wellness contexts sometimes invoke Samshin in discussions of maternal health and postpartum care.
lore.extendedMeditation: Samshin invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
